attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition matches the two causal sources he names: the prediction mechanism, and the model's own inability to look things up and reason. No hedge.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair. It treats 'inherent' as a structural source, not as total failure, and keeps the 'LLMs themselves' scope, which excludes external tools. The ambiguities are flagged properly.

evidence.note: Kalai & Vempala, March 2024 version. It gives a lower bound on hallucination from prediction, but only for calibrated LMs, and the authors say hallucination is not inevitable. It partly supports one component, mainly for pretrained models.
Google Research blog on ReAct (2022). A frozen PaLM uses an external Wikipedia interface. Because the lookup is external, it does not settle what 'LLMs themselves' can do.

reviews.rationale: e1 supports a structural, prediction-related source of hallucination, but only under calibration assumptions. It does not establish the claimed causes for the post-trained models Marcus discussed. e2 involves an external tool, so it neither refutes nor supports the unaided-LLM claim. The packet leaves the relative causal contributions open.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. The Hassabis mention that follows is separate context.

semantics.note: A general causal tendency, with the condition 'if expectations aren't met' kept. Not hedged.

contract.note: Reading 'fall' as a decline in valuations or investment, and the claim as an amplifying tendency, is ordinary in a post about a bubble. The bar of a causal comparison is demanding but fair.

evidence.note: A 2026 peer-reviewed study of AI washing and crash risk at Chinese listed firms (2010–2024). The topic is related, but it is broader than generative AI hype and does not compare declines after matched expectation misses.

reviews.rationale: The only admitted study links inflated AI claims to crash risk in a different population, using a different measure. It does not test whether greater prior generative AI hype causes larger falls after comparable disappointments. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The killer-app ranking keeps its 'probably' hedge. The income shortfall is stated firmly and is the checkable part.

contract.note: The contract reads costs as those attributable to the product. In context, Marcus may mean the industry's large chip and legal costs, a broader and arguably more natural reading. The contract flags this ambiguity, and the evidence settles neither reading.

evidence.note: A secondary report of a GitHub Copilot loss estimate for early 2023: one product, an earlier period, and later performance unknown. It cannot settle the claim for providers collectively through March 2024.
Microsoft's own disclosure of Copilot subscriber numbers. It gives no revenue or cost figures.

reviews.rationale: No matched revenue and cost figures for coding assistants exist in the packet, whether costs are read as product-attributable or industry-wide. One dated loss estimate and a subscriber count do not establish a shortfall or show that costs were covered by March 2024.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Two firm present-tense components: reliability, and a clear business model. Both are kept.

contract.note: The post is about costs and revenue, so 'clear business model' ordinarily means a clear viable way to make money. The contract instead counts any implemented revenue mechanism, such as one startup's subscription tier. That reading is stretched against the speaker. The reliability reading is fair.

evidence.note: An independent audit in March 2024 found material errors and poor sourcing on ordinary election questions, including in search-integrated Copilot. It supports the reliability component, within a narrow domain.
POLITICO report that dates the audit's testing to March 11–14, 2024. Corroboration, not a separate audit.

Reports that Perplexity had a subscription tier but was not profitable. That shows a revenue mechanism, not a clear viable business model for generative search, so it does not contradict the claim under a fair reading.

reviews.rationale: The reliability part holds: the March 2024 audit shows recurring material errors (e1, e2). The business-model part is not settled. One startup's unprofitable subscription does not show that generative search had a clear business model, and the contract's weaker reading, under which it counts as contradiction, is not fair to the speaker.
